credits.title: Credits
credits.body: Designed and built for NEXUS Cyber Academy. 3D rendering by three.js (MIT). All equipment, textures and sounds are generated procedurally in code. All scenarios, people, companies and IP addresses are fictional; IP addresses come from documentation-only ranges.
mission.s1.title: Brute force investigation
mission.s1.brief: The SIEM flagged unusual SSH activity on the web server srv-web-01 at 03:14. You have a shell on the server. Find who attacked it, find out whether they got in, and contain the incident. Start by reading the shift lead's note: `cat notes.txt`
mission.s1.obj.ip: Identify the attacking IP address (submit ip …)
mission.s1.obj.block: Block the attacker on the host firewall (ufw)
mission.s1.hint.1: Failed SSH logins are written to `/var/log/auth.log` with the phrase “Failed password”. Try: `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | head`
mission.s1.hint.2: Count failures per IP: `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`
mission.s1.hint.3: Look for a successful login from the same IP: `grep Accepted /var/log/auth.log`. Firewall and account changes need sudo: `sudo ufw deny from <ip>`, `sudo usermod -L <user>`.
mission.s1.debrief.1: A brute-force attack shows up in auth.log as many “Failed password” lines from one source in a short time. Counting failures per IP (`grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`) separates a real attack (142 attempts) from background noise (the 4-attempt scan and admins mistyping passwords).
mission.s1.debrief.2: The attacker eventually logged in as “backup”, a system account that had a password and a login shell. Attackers target accounts like this because nobody watches them.
mission.s1.debrief.3: Blocking the IP stops new attempts, but the account was already compromised, so you also had to lock it. Containment covers both the source and the foothold.
mission.s1.debrief.4: In production you would prevent this with key-only SSH (`PasswordAuthentication no`), fail2ban or rate limiting, MFA, and no login shell for service accounts — then investigate what “backup” did after 03:19.
fb.s1.notIp: That is not a valid IPv4 address.
fb.s1.ipCorrect: Correct — that IP is behind the attack.
fb.s1.decoy: Only 4 attempts from that IP before it gave up. That is internet background noise, not the attack.
fb.s1.internal: That address is in our internal 10.0.0.0/8 range — it is one of us.
fb.s1.ipWrong: That IP is not behind the attack. Count failed logins per IP.
fb.s1.userCorrect: Correct — the attacker logged in as “backup”.
fb.s1.root: root was targeted, but every attempt on it failed. Look for an “Accepted” login.
fb.s1.legit: That user logged in normally from the internal network.
fb.s1.userWrong: That account was not broken into. Look for a successful login from the attacker's IP.
fb.s1.blockedInternal: Warning: you just blocked an internal address. That could cut off a colleague.
fb.s1.blockedOther: Rule added, but that is not the attacking IP.
fb.s1.lockedWrong: That account was not compromised. Locking it could break a legitimate service or user.

mission.n1.title: Harden the access switch
mission.n1.brief: A visitor plugged a laptop into a free wall jack in the meeting room and got onto the office network. You are on the console of SW-ACCESS-01. Shut down every unused port, lock the reception port to the reception PC with port security, and save the configuration so it survives a reboot. Ports Fa0/1–Fa0/4 and Gi0/1 are in use; Fa0/5–Fa0/12 are unused wall jacks.
mission.n1.obj.unused: Shut down all unused ports (Fa0/5–Fa0/12) without cutting off devices in use
mission.n1.obj.portsec: Fa0/1: access mode + port security (max 1 MAC, sticky, violation shutdown)
mission.n1.obj.save: Save the running configuration to startup-config
mission.n1.hint.1: Start with `enable` then `show interfaces status` to see which ports are connected. To configure many ports at once: `configure terminal` then `interface range fa0/5 - 12` then `shutdown`.
mission.n1.hint.2: Port security only works on access ports. On `interface fa0/1`: `switchport mode access`, `switchport port-security`, `switchport port-security maximum 1`, `switchport port-security mac-address sticky`, `switchport port-security violation shutdown`.
mission.n1.hint.3: Changes live only in RAM until you save them. Leave config mode with `end`, then `copy running-config startup-config` (or `write memory`). Check your work with `show running-config` and `show port-security`.
mission.n1.debrief.1: Every unused port is a free network connection for anyone who walks by. Shutting them down (and enabling them only when needed) is one of the cheapest controls you can apply.
mission.n1.debrief.2: Port security with a sticky MAC learns the reception PC's address and shuts the port if any other device is plugged in. It stops casual plug-ins, but MAC addresses can be spoofed, so real networks add 802.1X authentication.
mission.n1.debrief.3: IOS refuses port security on a dynamic port because a port negotiating a trunk could carry many VLANs. Setting `switchport mode access` first is also a hardening step: it stops VLAN-hopping through DTP.
mission.n1.debrief.4: The running-config is lost on reboot unless you copy it to startup-config. Unsaved hardening is one of the most common findings in network audits.
fb.n1.cutOff: You shut down a port that a device is using. Bring it back with `no shutdown`.
fb.n1.maxHigh: Maximum above 1 lets extra devices share the reception port.
mission.c1.title: Fix the SQL injection
mission.c1.brief: A penetration test logged in as admin on the staff portal using the username `admin' --` and no password. The login function builds its SQL query by gluing user input into the string. Rewrite it so the database receives the values separately from the query, then run the security tests. Normal logins must keep working.
mission.c1.obj.works: Normal login (correct and wrong password) still works
mission.c1.hint.1: The problem is the + username + inside the SQL string. Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL command itself.
mission.c1.hint.2: Use placeholders in the query text: `WHERE username = ? AND password_hash = ?` and pass the values as the second argument of db.query.
mission.c1.hint.3: The fixed call looks like: `db.query(sql, [username, hash(password)])`. Keep the order of the values the same as the order of the placeholders.
mission.c1.debrief.1: With concatenation, the payload admin' -- closes the string and comments out the password check, so the query becomes “find user admin”. The database cannot tell your SQL apart from the attacker's.
mission.c1.debrief.2: Parameterized queries send the SQL and the values separately. The database compiles the query first and treats every value only as data, so quotes and comments in a username are harmless.
mission.c1.debrief.3: Filtering or escaping quotes yourself is fragile: encodings, other quote characters and second-order injection get past it. Placeholders are the fix; input validation is an extra layer, not a replacement.
mission.c1.debrief.4: The same rule applies in every language and driver: PreparedStatement in Java, cursor.execute(sql, params) in Python, PDO prepared statements in PHP, and ORMs that bind values for you.
fb.c1.still: The tests still bypass the login. User input is still part of the SQL text.
fb.c1.filter: Filtering characters does not fix SQL injection. Use placeholders and pass the values separately.
fb.c1.broken: Injection is blocked, but normal login no longer works. Check the placeholders and the values array.
mission.k1.title: Exposed storage bucket
mission.k1.brief: A security researcher reported that one of the company's storage buckets is readable by anyone on the internet and contains employee data. You have the NexusCloud CLI on the bastion host. Find the bucket, make it private, and turn on encryption — without taking down the public website, which is also served from storage.
mission.k1.hint.1: List buckets with `nxcloud storage ls`, then look inside each one with `nxcloud storage ls <bucket>`. Check who can read it with `nxcloud storage get-bucket-policy <bucket>`.
mission.k1.hint.2: Two buckets are public. Only one of them should be: the website. Which one holds payroll and bank data?
mission.k1.hint.3: Lock it down with `nxcloud storage put-public-access-block <bucket> --block-all`, then `nxcloud storage put-encryption <bucket> --algorithm AES256`.
mission.k1.debrief.1: A policy with Principal "*" means anyone on the internet. Misconfigured storage like this is behind many of the largest real-world data leaks — no hacking needed, just a URL.
mission.k1.debrief.2: A public access block is a guardrail on top of the policy: even if someone later adds a public policy by mistake, the block keeps the bucket private.
mission.k1.debrief.3: Not every public bucket is a problem — the website is meant to be public. Security work means understanding the purpose of each resource before changing it, so you don't cause an outage while fixing a leak.
mission.k1.debrief.4: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks and some provider-side access, but it would not have stopped this leak: the data was served decrypted to anyone allowed to read it. Access control comes first.
fb.k1.found: Correct — that bucket holds payroll and bank data and is public.
fb.k1.websiteIntended: That bucket is public on purpose: it serves the company website.
fb.k1.notPublic: That bucket is not publicly readable.
fb.k1.noSuch: There is no bucket with that name.
fb.k1.websiteDown: Warning: you just made the website bucket private. The public website is now down.
mission.f1.title: Evidence integrity
mission.f1.brief: In a procurement fraud case, the defense claims the digital evidence was altered after it was seized. The hashes of every file were recorded at seizure. Verify the evidence folder, find the file that changed, and use its metadata to find which account modified it.
mission.f1.obj.file: Find the file that no longer matches its recorded hash
mission.f1.obj.user: Find the account that last modified it
mission.f1.hint.1: Read `cat custody.txt`, then look at the recorded hashes with `cat SHA256SUMS`. Compute a file's hash with `sha256sum <file>`.
mission.f1.hint.2: Check every file at once: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`.
mission.f1.hint.3: Metadata shows who edited a document: `exiftool <file>`. Look for “Last Modified By” and compare the Modify Date with the seizure time.
mission.f1.debrief.1: A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint: changing one character produces a completely different SHA-256. Recording hashes at seizure is how investigators prove evidence was not changed afterwards.
mission.f1.debrief.2: The invoice amount was raised from 48,500 to 148,500 and the bank account was changed — the hash mismatch proves the file is not the one that was seized.
mission.f1.debrief.3: The metadata shows the edit happened at 23:47 on 31 October, after seizure, by m.farouk. Metadata is useful but can be forged, so investigators corroborate it with logs and other sources.
mission.f1.debrief.4: Chain of custody — who held the evidence, when, and how it was protected — is what makes digital evidence admissible. Write blockers, hashing and sealed storage all serve that goal.
fb.f1.fileOk: Correct — that file's hash does not match.
fb.f1.fileWrong: That file still matches its recorded hash.
fb.f1.userOk: Correct — that account modified the file after seizure.
fb.f1.author: That account created the document. Look for who modified it last.
fb.f1.userWrong: That is not the account in the file's metadata.
mission.x1.title: Decode the intercept
mission.x1.brief: A message was intercepted from a compromised mail server. The suspects believe it is encrypted, but it is only encoded in several layers. Peel the layers off one by one with terminal tools to recover the proof string and the meeting time.
mission.x1.obj.flag: Recover the proof string (submit flag NEXUS{…})
mission.x1.obj.time: Find the meeting time (submit time HH:MM)
mission.x1.hint.1: Look at the file: `cat intercept.txt`. Only the characters 0–9 and a–f? That is hex. Turn hex back into bytes with `xxd -r -p`.
mission.x1.hint.2: The result ends with = and uses A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /: that is Base64. Chain it: `cat intercept.txt | xxd -r -p | base64 -d`.
mission.x1.hint.3: The text now looks like letters shifted by 13 places (ARKHF instead of NEXUS): that is ROT13. Add `| tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'`.
mission.x1.debrief.1: Hex, Base64 and ROT13 are encodings, not encryption: there is no key. Anyone who recognizes the format can reverse it, which is why stacking them adds almost no security.
mission.x1.debrief.2: Recognizing formats is a core skill: hex uses only 0–9 and a–f, Base64 uses A–Z a–z 0–9 + / and often ends with =, and ROT13 keeps word shapes but scrambles letters.
mission.x1.debrief.3: Real encryption (AES, ChaCha20) uses a secret key; without it, the output looks random and cannot be peeled off with tools like these.
mission.x1.debrief.4: Attackers and malware use layered encoding to slip past simple filters. Analysts decode it step by step exactly like this, often with tools such as CyberChef.
fb.x1.flagWrong: That is not the proof string.
fb.x1.stillRot: Close — that is still ROT13. Shift the letters back by 13.
fb.x1.timeWrong: That is not the meeting time in the message.
mission.s2.title: Phishing analysis
mission.s2.brief: Staff reported four suspicious emails. Only one is malicious. Inspect the raw headers and the links, identify the phishing email and the attacker's real domain, then pull it from every mailbox — without removing legitimate mail.
mission.s2.obj.domain: Identify the attacker's real domain (submit domain …)
mission.s2.hint.1: List the emails with `ls reported` and read them with `cat`. Look at the headers above the body, not only at the From line.
mission.s2.hint.2: Compare `grep -H Received-SPF reported/*` across all emails, and compare each link's text with its actual URL.
mission.s2.hint.3: The From header can be forged. The real domain appears in Return-Path, Reply-To and the actual link URL.
mission.s2.debrief.1: The From line said microsoft.com, but SPF failed: the sending server was not allowed to send for that domain. The Return-Path, Reply-To and the real link all pointed to a lookalike domain with a zero instead of an o.
mission.s2.debrief.2: Urgency (“suspended in 24h”), a mismatch between link text and real URL, and a login page on a strange domain are the classic signs of credential phishing.
mission.s2.debrief.3: The password-expiry email looked scary but was legitimate: internal sender, SPF and DKIM pass, and links to the real portal. Checking evidence instead of reacting to tone avoids deleting real mail.
fb.s2.emailOk: Correct — that is the phishing email.
fb.s2.emailWrong: That email looks legitimate. Check the headers.
fb.s2.decoy: Scary subject, but SPF and DKIM pass and the link goes to our own portal. It's legitimate.
fb.s2.spoofed: That's the forged From address. Find where replies and links really go.
fb.s2.quarantined: Phishing email removed from all mailboxes.
fb.s2.quarantineWrong: You removed a legitimate email from 412 mailboxes.
mission.n2.title: Segment the network with VLANs
mission.n2.brief: The guest Wi-Fi access point (Fa0/4) and the finance PC (Fa0/2) are on the same VLAN, so a guest can reach finance. Create VLAN 20 named FINANCE and VLAN 30 named GUEST, move each port into its VLAN, leave the reception PC, the printer and the trunk uplink as they are, and save.
mission.n2.obj.assign: Fa0/2 → VLAN 20, Fa0/4 → VLAN 30, other ports unchanged
mission.n2.hint.1: `enable`, `conf t`, then `vlan 20` and `name FINANCE`. Do the same for VLAN 30.
mission.n2.hint.2: Assign a port with `interface fa0/2` then `switchport access vlan 20`. Check with `show vlan brief`.
mission.n2.hint.3: Don't touch Gi0/1: it is a trunk that carries all VLANs to the core. Finish with `end` and `write memory`.
mission.n2.debrief.1: VLANs split one physical switch into separate broadcast domains. Devices in different VLANs can only talk through a router or firewall, where rules can be enforced.
mission.n2.debrief.2: Putting guests in their own VLAN is a basic segmentation step: if a guest device is compromised, it can no longer reach finance machines directly.
mission.n2.debrief.3: The uplink stays a trunk so traffic for every VLAN can reach the core switch and the firewall that routes between them.
fb.n2.wrongPort: That device should stay in VLAN 1. Put it back with `switchport access vlan 1`.
fb.n2.trunk: Gi0/1 must stay a trunk, or the other VLANs lose their path to the core.
mission.k2.title: Cryptominer on the web server
mission.k2.brief: A production web server has run at 98% CPU for six hours and the cloud bill jumped. Find what is eating the CPU, stop it, make sure it cannot come back, delete it, and find the server it downloads itself from.
mission.k2.hint.1: `ps aux` shows every process with its CPU usage. The odd one runs from /tmp, a strange place for a program.
mission.k2.hint.2: If it comes back after you kill it, something restarts it. Check the web user's scheduled jobs: `sudo crontab -u www-data -l`.
mission.k2.hint.3: Order matters: `sudo crontab -u www-data -r`, then `sudo kill <pid>`, then `sudo rm -r /tmp/.x`. The download server is in the cron line and the nginx access log.
mission.k2.debrief.1: Attackers uploaded a web shell, then used it to download a cryptominer. Mining burns your CPU and your money; it is one of the most common payloads on exposed servers.
mission.k2.debrief.2: Killing the process alone is not enough: the cron job restarted it every few minutes. Always look for persistence — cron, systemd services, startup scripts — before you clean up.
mission.k2.debrief.3: Cleaning is only containment. The root cause is the vulnerable upload page; in a real incident you would also rebuild the server from a clean image and rotate its credentials.
fb.k2.killedCronLeft: Process stopped… for now. Something might restart it.
fb.k2.respawn: The miner is back with a new PID. Something restarted it.
fb.k2.rmRunning: File deleted, but the process is still running in memory.
fb.k2.uploader: That IP uploaded the web shell. Where does the cron job download from?
mission.c2.title: Fix the cross-site scripting
mission.c2.brief: A student posted a comment containing HTML and JavaScript, and it ran in every visitor's browser on the lesson page. The render function inserts user input as HTML. Make it display comments as plain text, then run the security tests.
mission.c2.obj.xss: All XSS payloads are displayed as text
mission.c2.obj.works: Normal comments still show author and text
mission.c2.hint.1: `innerHTML` parses whatever you give it as HTML — including script tags and event handlers.
mission.c2.hint.2: Build the elements yourself and set text with `textContent`, which never parses HTML.
mission.c2.hint.3: For example: create a `strong` element, set `strong.textContent = comment.author`, append it, then append `document.createTextNode(': ' + comment.text)`.
mission.c2.debrief.1: Stored XSS runs attacker JavaScript in every visitor's browser: it can steal session cookies, act as the user, or rewrite the page.
mission.c2.debrief.2: `textContent` and `createTextNode` treat input as text, so `<script>` is shown, not executed. When you must build HTML, escape every untrusted value — both fields, not just one.
mission.c2.debrief.3: Defense in depth: frameworks that escape by default, a Content-Security-Policy header, and HttpOnly cookies all limit the damage if one spot is missed.
fb.c2.still: Payloads still execute. User input still reaches innerHTML as HTML.
fb.c2.partial: Only one field is protected. The attacker can use the other one.
fb.c2.broken: Safe now, but the comment no longer shows correctly.
mission.f2.title: Insider timeline
mission.f2.brief: The payroll file was copied to a USB stick from a finance office PC on the night of 3 November. The file server log names an account — but an account is not a person. Correlate the file server, badge and VPN logs to find who was really sitting at that PC.
mission.f2.obj.account: Identify the account that copied the file
mission.f2.obj.suspect: Identify the person physically at the PC
mission.f2.hint.1: Find the copy event first: `grep COPY fileserver.log`. Note the time, account and host.
mission.f2.hint.2: Was that person even in the building? `grep s.adel badge.log`. FIN-WS-07 cannot be used over VPN.
mission.f2.hint.3: Look at who entered the finance office shortly before 22:41: `grep FINANCE badge.log`.
mission.f2.debrief.1: The copy was made with s.adel's account, but s.adel had badged out at 18:05 and had no VPN session — and the PC is only usable in person.
mission.f2.debrief.2: k.hamdy badged into the finance office at 22:30 and left at 22:47, bracketing the 22:41 copy. The account was used by someone else, probably with a password seen or left on a note.
mission.f2.debrief.3: Timelines built from several independent sources are much stronger than any single log. This is also why shared or written-down passwords make investigations so hard.
fb.f2.accountOk: Correct — that account performed the copy.
fb.f2.accountWrong: The file server log shows a different account.
fb.f2.suspectOk: Correct — the badge records place them in the finance office at the time.
fb.f2.wasHome: The account owner had already left the building and had no VPN session.
fb.f2.serverRoom: That person was in the server room, not the finance office.
fb.f2.vpn: That person was only connected remotely, and this PC isn't reachable over VPN.
fb.f2.suspectWrong: The logs don't place that person at the PC.
mission.x2.title: Weak passwords
mission.x2.brief: A partner portal leaked its password database. The passwords were stored as plain, unsalted SHA-256 hashes. Run a dictionary attack to measure the damage: find the admin's password and how many accounts fall.
mission.x2.obj.cracked: Find how many accounts can be cracked
mission.x2.hint.1: Run `crack leak/users.sha256 leak/wordlist.txt` and see what falls.
mission.x2.hint.2: The admin isn't cracked yet. Look at the wordlist: people change passwords in predictable ways (new year, extra symbol).
mission.x2.debrief.1: Fast, unsalted hashes let an attacker test millions of guesses per second, and identical passwords produce identical hashes across all users.
mission.x2.debrief.2: Rules turn Summer2025! into Summer2026! instantly. “Changing the year” is not a new password. Long random passphrases (like n.farid's) survive.
mission.x2.debrief.3: Store passwords with a slow, salted algorithm — bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 — and add MFA so a cracked password alone is not enough.
fb.x2.pwOk: Correct — the admin password is cracked.
fb.x2.almost: Close! That's in the wordlist, but the admin changed it slightly.
fb.x2.pwWrong: That is not the admin's password.
fb.x2.countOk: Correct — that many accounts fall to a simple attack.
fb.x2.useRules: That's without rules. Real attackers always add mangling rules.
fb.x2.countWrong: That number doesn't match what the attack recovers.

esc.warden.1: The note and the printout belong together. Which service on the printout is still waiting for its patch?
esc.warden.2: `ls` only shows what wants to be seen. Try `ls -a`, then decode what you find.
esc.warden.3: The crash screens have timestamps. Earliest failure first.

mission.esc2.title: Vault terminal
mission.esc2.hint.1: Start with `cat README`. Is that really everything in this folder?
mission.esc2.hint.2: `ls -a` shows hidden files. The content looks like Base64: `base64 -d <file>`.

esc.vault.desc: Ports, hidden files and power. The classic.

esc.binary.desc: Think like a machine: bits, counts and dependencies.
esc.cipher.title: Cipher Room
esc.cipher.desc: Old ciphers, fingerprints and a riddle.
esc.binary.note: “I changed the PIN again. It's on the printout — read it like a computer would. — IT”
esc.binary.board: Binary cheat sheet: place values 8 4 2 1. Example: 0101 = 4 + 1 = 5.
esc.binary.label: “Count, don't guess.” (someone wrote: sort | uniq -c)
esc.binary.warden.1: Each line on the printout is one digit, written in base 2.
esc.binary.warden.2: Count failures per user: `awk '{print $5}' auth_failures.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`.
esc.binary.warden.3: The crash screens say what each rack does and what it depends on. Start with the one that depends on nothing.
mission.esc2b.title: Vault terminal
mission.esc2b.hint.1: Read `cat README`. Which account failed the most?
esc.cipher.note: “Julius left the new code on the whiteboard. He always shifts by three.”
esc.cipher.board: Whiteboard: WKUHH RQH ILYH QLQH — J.C.
esc.cipher.label: “Trust, but verify.” (someone wrote: sha256sum)
esc.cipher.plaque: “The first to fall is the last to rise.”
esc.cipher.warden.1: A Caesar shift of 3: D means A, E means B… Decode the words, then turn them into digits.
esc.cipher.warden.2: Hash every key file: `sha256sum key1 key2 key3 key4`, and compare with door.sha256.
esc.cipher.warden.3: Look at the crash times. The one that failed first comes back last.
mission.esc2c.title: Vault terminal
mission.esc2c.hint.2: `sha256sum key1 key2 key3 key4` — the matching file holds the key.
ra.title: RED ALERT drill
ra.brief: Ransomware is spreading through the academy network. You have 15 minutes to find patient zero (SOC), isolate it (Network), stop the attackers deleting backups (Cloud) and restore from a clean backup (Forensics). Each step happens in a different lab — run.
ra.task.1: find patient zero in the SOC
ra.task.2: isolate the host in Network Security
ra.task.3: disable the stolen key in Cloud Security
ra.task.4: restore a clean backup in Digital Forensics
ra.wrongLab: RED ALERT: the next step is in {lab}.
ra.win.title: Outbreak contained!
ra.win.body: Patient zero found, isolated, the stolen key disabled and the file server restored. Time: {t}.
ra.fail.title: Time's up
ra.fail.body: The ransomware reached the backups. Try the drill again — you'll know the path this time.
ra.fb.notFirst: That host was infected, but not first. Look at the timestamps.
ra.fb.wrongPort: You cut off a healthy device. Only the infected host should go dark.
ra.fb.ciKey: That's the CI deploy key — deployments just stopped. Re-check which key the attacker used.
ra.fb.restored: File server restored from a clean backup.
ra.fb.encrypted: That backup is encrypted by the ransomware.
ra.fb.tooOld: That one is clean, but a newer clean backup exists — you'd lose a day of work.
mission.ra1.title: RED ALERT 1/4 — Patient zero
mission.ra1.obj.host: Find the first infected host (submit host …)
mission.ra1.hint.1: `cat edr_alerts.log` — the lines are not in time order.
mission.ra1.hint.2: `sort edr_alerts.log` puts them in time order. Which host shows up first?
mission.ra2.title: RED ALERT 2/4 — Isolate
mission.ra2.obj.isolate: Shut down only the infected host's port
mission.ra2.hint.1: `enable`, then `show interfaces status` to find the port named after the infected host.
mission.ra3.title: RED ALERT 3/4 — Stolen key
mission.ra3.obj.key: Disable the stolen access key (keep the CI key)
mission.ra3.hint.1: `cat audit.log` — which key is used from an outside IP to delete backups?
mission.ra4.title: RED ALERT 4/4 — Restore
mission.ra4.hint.1: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` shows which backups are intact.
mission.ra4.hint.2: Pick the newest one that says OK: `restore <file>`.
